To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the size of the merit pay raise received by hospital employees was positively related to their happiness and effort intentions, but not to their pay level satisfaction; and 2) the size of merit pay raise was more strongly related to happiness and effort intentions for employees who were low rather than high in trait positive affectivity.
the size of the merit pay raise was more strongly related to happiness and effort intentions among those low on trait PA than those high on trait PA, but not for pay satisfaction.

the relationship between the amount of merit pay raise received and reactions to the raise (happiness and intentions to work hard) is stronger among individuals who have lower trait positive affectivity than among those who have higher levels of trait positive affectivity.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the relationship among merit pay increases and reactions to merit increases, and the role of trait positive affectivity as a moderator of the relationship between merit increase size and reactions to increases.
how people respond to the size of their merit pay raises.
the relationship between the amount of a pay raise and reactions to that raise.

the signal sensitivity perspective can provide useful insights into reactions to merit pay raises.

the relationship between merit raise and employee reactions to it is not straightforward. It depends not only on the raise amount, but also on employees’ PA.
